extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers of British television and medical drama
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and descriptive aspects for assessing or producing a British medical drama television series, drawn from a Wikipedia article on Cardiac Arrest. Covers tone, realism, thematic portrayals (racism, sexism, homophobia), depiction of medical roles, production details and reception/impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic and gritty portrayal of the medical profession
rubrics_metrics.description: The show was known for its realistic and sometimes dark portrayal of the medical profession; Mercurio's experiences as a doctor influenced the realistic and often gritty portrayal of the medical profession in the series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity is achieved by drawing on real medical experience; tone is visceral and sometimes wryly humorous. This realism contributed to the series topping polls of the UK medical profession as a top medical drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cynical/controversial depiction of doctors, nurses and the NHS
rubrics_metrics.description: The series was controversial owing to its cynical depiction of doctors, nurses and the National Health Service (NHS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversy is an expected outcome when a drama depicts healthcare professionals and institutions cynically; reactions included complaints (e.g., from Royal College of Nursing) and public/political comments (e.g., Health Secretary describing it as closer to a Carry On film).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: dark humour combined with disturbing themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Although billed as a comedy, and darkly humorous in many respects, Cardiac Arrest explores several disturbing themes and did not attempt to be politically correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing dark humour with disturbing subject matter is a deliberate stylistic choice; the show 'demolishes many cherished concepts of healthcare' and attracts both support (junior doctors) and complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of racism as endemic in the health service
rubrics_metrics.description: Cardiac Arrest is stark in its portrayal of racist attitudes, which are depicted as endemic throughout the health service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include assumptions about competence based on nationality and exclusion from opportunities (e.g., surgeons with 'foreign' names not chosen). Use of such portrayals serves thematic critique but also invites scrutiny of representation accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of sexism and sexual harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Female patients and staff are portrayed as subject to continual sexual harassment; scenes depict systems where reporting harassment risks job loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portraying sexism includes showing consequences for victims and institutional pressures that suppress complaints; useful as critique of workplace culture but must be contextualised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of homophobia and HIV-related stigma
rubrics_metrics.description: The series depicts homophobia and the stigma surrounding HIV — e.g., the leak of a doctor's HIV diagnosis leads to scandal and accusation, and a character is later falsely accused of child abuse influenced by homophobic attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic storylines show personal and institutional responses to sexuality and disease, highlighting systemic prejudice and media-leak risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of junior doctors' working conditions and ethos
rubrics_metrics.description: Junior doctors are shown as overworked, required to do menial tasks, exposed to excessive hours (three days on call), subject to hazing, and emotionally strained — 'junior hospital medicine as an unending parade' with few stable relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on workload, lack of supervision, hazing practices, and moral consequences of training-as-abuse; these elements support critique of medical training and workplace culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of consultants (senior doctors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultants are mostly portrayed as callous and uncaring toward patients and staff, often absent from ward duties and protective of their status; some senior doctors are shown more sympathetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depicting a range of senior clinician behaviours supports narrative conflict (neglect, blame-shifting, bullying) and allows some counterexamples (supportive consultants) for nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of managers and managerial priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers are portrayed with considerable venom: more interested in protecting jobs and improving metrics (e.g., outpatient waiting times) than staff working conditions or patient care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managerial characters are used to critique managerialism and metric-driven decision-making; storylines include budget cuts, PR teams, and political maneuvering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of nurses (from caricature to more complex later)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Series 1 nurses are frequently shown as gossiping, conniving and neglectful; in later series senior nurses become more central and portrayed more positively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character arcs can move from caricature to depth over series; be aware of professional associations' reactions (e.g., Royal College of Nursing complaint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical stance on medical training and hazing
rubrics_metrics.description: The series is extremely critical of medical training, portraying it as unduly demanding, inadequately supervised, and including hazing practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative to highlight systemic training failures and ethical consequences; specific scenes/dialogue discuss hazing and the 'school of hard knocks' nature of junior medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of creator's medical experience and technical advising to ensure authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Creator Jed Mercurio's prior work as a doctor influenced the series; he served as technical medical adviser for series 2 and 'production consultant' for series 3, giving access to hands-on production processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involving practitioners as writers/advisers is presented as central to achieving verisimilitude and credible portrayals; credited as Mercurio's apprenticeship in producing/directing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production and format specifics (runtime, series/episode counts, filming locations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Running time: 30 minutes; No. of series: 3; No. of episodes: 27 (series 1:6, series 2:8, series 3:13); filmed on location at Ruchill and Stobhill Hospitals in Glasgow; produced by World Productions for BBC One.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete production constraints and choices that shape storytelling (short runtime, episodic structure, location filming) and are relevant when producing comparable series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception, awards recognition and impact (including debates about factual claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical response was generally positive; nominations by Writers' Guild of Great Britain and BAFTA Scotland; doctors reported it representative; it originated the term 'killing season' though medical data do not support the concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure impact by critical nominations, practitioner polls/support, controversies, and influence on public discourse (e.g., coinage of terms). Also note empirical counter-evidence (BMJ conclusion that 'killing season' is fiction; later studies about Black Wednesday show small effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution and re-release considerations (DVD release and later repeats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete series released as a five-disc DVD set (no extras) in 2007; repeated on BBC Four and made available on BBC iPlayer in 2023 with an interview with Mercurio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability formats and extras (or lack thereof) affect audience reach and scholarly/review interest; re-broadcasts and contemporaneous interviews can renew critical reassessment.
